prompt: After three clicks on Toggle, what did the HTML of `#panels` hold where the `v-if` paragraph had been?
hint: Look at the last line of the transcript.

choices.text: The paragraph, with `style="display: none;"`
choices.why: That is the `v-show` paragraph. `v-if` takes the element off the page instead of hiding it.

choices.text: Nothing whatsoever
choices.why: Vue leaves something behind: it needs to know where to put the element back when the condition turns true.

choices.text: A comment, `<!--v-if-->`
choices.why: Right. The comment is a placeholder that marks where the element goes back.

choices.text: The paragraph, with a `hidden` attribute on it
choices.why: Neither directive uses `hidden`. `v-show` sets `display: none`, and `v-if` removes the element.

prompt: In the transcript of three toggles, how many times was the `with v-if` component created?
hint: Count the lines that end in `created`.

prompt: A notes panel holds a half-typed note, and the student opens and closes it dozens of times in one sitting. By the lesson's table, which fits it?
hint: Two rows of the table decide this one: the cost of a toggle and what happens to state inside.

choices.text: `v-if`, because building nothing is the cheapest
choices.why: That is the default for things that stay hidden. Here every toggle would rebuild the panel and lose the half-typed note.

choices.text: `v-if` on a `<template>`, so that no wrapper is added to the page
choices.why: The `<template>` only saves a wrapper element. Underneath it is still `v-if`, and the note is still lost when the panel closes.

choices.text: Either one: for a screen reader they are the same
choices.why: They are the same for a screen reader, and that is the one row where they agree. The state inside is where they differ.

choices.text: `v-show`, so the note survives and a toggle changes one style
choices.why: Right. Toggled often, and with state that has to survive being hidden: both are the reasons the lesson gives for `v-show`.

prompt: What did `{{ n }} ` put on the page?
hint: A range in `v-for` does not count the way an array index does.

choices.why: That is how an index counts. A range starts at 1.
That would be a range starting at 0 and including 3. It starts at 1 and stops at 3.
Right. A range starts at 1, the one place in Vue where counting does.

choices.text: Nothing, because a number is not a list
choices.why: `v-for` repeats over a number as a range; the transcript printed three digits.

prompt: `<li v-for="session in sessions" v-if="session.done">` left the page empty in Vue 3. Why?
hint: Which of the two directives ran first?

choices.text: `v-if` ran first, before `session` existed
choices.why: Right. The warning says `session` was accessed during render but is not defined, and reading `.done` of undefined threw.

choices.text: `v-for` ran first, and the filter left no session to show
choices.why: That is Vue 2's order. One of the two sessions is done, so a filter that ran after the loop would have shown it.

choices.text: An element with `v-if` may not carry a `:key`
choices.why: The errors are about `session` being undefined, not about the key.

choices.text: The `done` property is missing from the data
choices.why: Both sessions have `done`. What was missing was `session` itself, at the moment `v-if` asked.

prompt: Which of these show only the sessions that are done, the way the lesson accepts? Choose all that apply.
hint: One way gives the filtered list a name; the other filters inside the loop.

choices.text: `v-for` and `v-if` together on the `<li>`
choices.why: That is the demo that left the page empty: in Vue 3 the `v-if` runs first.

choices.text: A `computed` that filters, and a plain `v-for` over it
choices.why: Right. The filtered list means something, so it gets a name in the script.

choices.text: A `v-if="session.done"` on the `<ul>` around the loop
choices.why: The `<ul>` is outside the loop, where no `session` exists, and it would hide the whole list rather than single rows.

choices.text: `<template v-for>` with the `v-if` on the `<li>` inside it
choices.why: Right. The loop runs first and each copy then decides, which is how the first demo's last list does it.

prompt: Statistics was starred in the list keyed by index, then removed from the courses. Which component did Vue remove from that list?
hint: Ask which keys exist before the removal and which exist after.

choices.text: The one with key 0, which held the star
choices.why: Key 0 still exists after the removal, so its component stays, star included. That is why Spanish shows a star.

choices.text: None of them; Vue rebuilt all three rows
choices.why: If every row had been rebuilt, the star would have vanished. It moved to Spanish because a component was kept.

choices.text: The one with key 2
choices.why: Right. Only keys 0 and 1 remain, so the last component went, though it had nothing to do with statistics.

choices.text: The statistics component, wherever it was
choices.why: That is what happened in the list keyed by course. Keyed by index, Vue does not know which component was statistics.

prompt: A list of notes is keyed by index, and each row has a text field. The student half-types into the first row, then a new note is inserted at the top of the list. Where is the half-typed text now?
hint: The text belongs to the element, not to the list.

choices.text: Beside its own note, now in the second row
choices.why: That is what a stable key would give. With an index, Vue reuses the elements by position.

choices.text: Still in the first row, beside the new note
choices.why: Right. Key 0 survived, so its element and the text in it stayed at position 0 while the notes moved past.

choices.text: Gone, because inserting rebuilds every row
choices.why: Vue keeps every component whose key still exists, and all the old keys still exist. Only one new row is built.

choices.text: Nowhere: Vue warns that two rows share key 0 and draws nothing
choices.why: Indexes are unique, so no two rows share a key. The problem with an index is that it is not stable.

prompt: Which of these make a good `:key` for a row of the planner's sessions? Choose all that apply.
hint: Stable, unique among its siblings, and a string or a number.

choices.text: `session.id`
choices.why: Right. It never changes and no two sessions share one.

choices.text: `session.date`
choices.why: It is a string, but it is not unique: two sessions fall on 19 October.

choices.text: The session object itself
choices.why: A key is a string or a number. Two objects never compare equal as keys, so a replaced list would match nothing.

choices.text: A number given to each session when it is created and never reused
choices.why: Right. That is what `addSession` does with the next number: stable and unique.

choices.text: The `index` from `(session, index) in thisWeek`
choices.why: The list is sorted by date, so a session added later moves every index after it.

prompt: An index is acceptable as a key only when the list never changes ___ and its rows hold no state of their own.
hint: Sorting is what breaks it.

prompt: Two checkboxes, `reading` and `exercises`, share `v-model="kinds"`. After ticking only Exercises, what did `kinds` hold?
hint: Several checkboxes with one array.

choices.text: `true`
choices.why: That is what a lone checkbox gives. Bound to an array, checkboxes give the values that are ticked.

choices.text: `[ false, true ]`
choices.why: The array does not hold one flag per box; it holds the `value` of each box that is ticked.

choices.text: `"exercises"`, a string on its own
choices.why: One chosen value as a string is what radio buttons give.

choices.text: `[ "exercises" ]`
choices.why: Right. The array of the `value`s that are ticked, and only one is.

prompt: `note` is a ref holding `''`, and the template has `<input v-model="note" value="hello">`. What does the field show when the page loads?
hint: Which of the two is the truth?

choices.text: `hello`, and `note` becomes `'hello'`
choices.why: The attribute does not write into the ref. Initial values go in the ref.

choices.text: An empty field, whatever `value` says
choices.why: Right. The ref is the truth, and the field's own `value` attribute is ignored.

choices.text: `hello`, until the student starts typing
choices.why: That is plain HTML's behaviour. With `v-model` the field shows whatever `note` holds from the start.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because Vue refuses to compile the template
choices.why: The lesson says the attribute is ignored, not refused; the page renders with the ref's value.

prompt: Why does the planner's list not put `v-model` on `session.done`?
hint: Lesson 3 decided how the list of sessions changes.

choices.text: `v-model` does not work on a checkbox
choices.why: It does: a lone checkbox gives `true` or `false`, as the `Done` box in the demo showed.

choices.text: It would flip the property inside the list in place, behind `toggleDone`'s back
choices.why: Right. The planner's rule is that the list is replaced through `toggleDone`, never changed in place.

choices.text: On a checkbox it listens to `input`, on every keystroke
choices.why: A checkbox's `v-model` listens to `change`. The event was never the problem.

choices.text: Inside a `v-for` it reaches only the loop's copy, never the list
choices.why: The loop variable is the object in the list itself, which is exactly why writing into it would change the list in place.

prompt: In the transcript of BindAndOn, Enter was pressed in the minutes field. Which line came first, and why?
hint: When does a browser submit a form: the key going down or coming up?

choices.text: `Enter pressed`, because `keyup` fires before the form is submitted
choices.why: The order was the other way round: the submit happens on the key going down, before it comes up.

choices.text: `submitted 60 minutes…`, because a browser submits a form on the key going down
choices.why: Right. The `keyup` handler ran after, when the key came back up.

choices.text: `submitted 60 minutes…`, because `.prevent` holds the `keyup` handler back
choices.why: `.prevent` calls `preventDefault()` on the submit event and nothing else; it does not delay other listeners.

choices.text: Only `Enter pressed`; `.prevent` stopped the submit handler from running
choices.why: `.prevent` stops the browser's default, the page load, and the handler still runs: the transcript printed both lines.

prompt: A button has `:disabled="saving"`, and `saving` is `false`. What is on the button in the HTML?
hint: A bound `false` on a boolean attribute.

choices.text: `disabled="false"`, which still disables it
choices.why: That is the trap of writing the attribute by hand in HTML. A bound `false` removes a boolean attribute.

choices.text: `disabled=""`, until `saving` turns true
choices.why: An empty `disabled` is still disabled. The attribute is removed until `saving` is true.

choices.text: No `disabled` attribute
choices.why: Right. `false` removes a boolean attribute, so the button is enabled, which is why the idiom works.

choices.text: `disabled`, because any bound value sets a boolean attribute
choices.why: Only `null` and `undefined` remove every attribute, but `false` removes a boolean one such as `disabled` too.

prompt: The modifier that keeps a submitted form from loading its address again is written `@submit.___`.
hint: It calls the event's method of the same name, before the handler.

prompt: A click handler on a button should run the first time only, and the click should not reach the button's parents. Which modifiers does it need? Choose all that apply.
hint: One removes the listener, one stops the bubbling.

choices.text: `.once`
choices.why: Right. The listener is removed after the first time.

choices.text: `.self`
choices.why: `.self` decides which clicks run this handler, those on the element and not a child; it does not stop the event bubbling up.

choices.text: `.stop`
choices.why: Right. `event.stopPropagation()`: the event does not bubble to the parents.

choices.text: `.prevent`
choices.why: `.prevent` stops the browser's default action, such as a form loading a page; the event still bubbles.

prompt: In FocusDirective, the focus went to `#minutes` rather than `#course`. Why?
hint: Where does `v-focus` sit?

choices.text: Vue focuses the last field of a component when it mounts
choices.why: Vue focuses nothing on its own. Something had to call `focus()`.

choices.text: `v-focus` sits on `#minutes`, and its `mounted` hook focused that element
choices.why: Right. The hook ran with the element it sits on, once it was on the page.

choices.text: The `onMounted` in the script moved the focus there
choices.why: That `onMounted` only prints where the focus is. It reads `document.activeElement`; it does not set it.

choices.text: The directive ran on every input, and the last to mount kept the focus
choices.why: A directive acts on the element it is written on, and only `#minutes` has `v-focus`.

prompt: In `<script setup>`, which variable is available in the template as `v-colour`, with nothing registered?
hint: The naming rule: a letter, then a capital.

choices.text: `useColour`
choices.why: `use` is the naming habit of a composable. A directive's name starts with `v` and a capital.

choices.text: `colour`
choices.why: Without the `v` prefix it is an ordinary variable; it would have to be registered with `app.directive` to be one.

choices.text: `v_colour`
choices.why: The rule is `v` followed by a capital letter, as in `vFocus`, not an underscore.

choices.text: `vColour`
choices.why: Right. `v` followed by a capital letter, used in the template as `v-colour`.

prompt: In the transcript of the planner, how many minutes of Spanish were planned for the week of 19 October?
hint: Add the two Spanish sessions in the list, or read the course's line.

prompt: A checkbox has its text beside it, but outside any `<label>` and not tied to one with `for` and `id`. What does a screen reader announce for it?
hint: The name of a checkbox comes from its label.

choices.text: The text beside it, as the box's name
choices.why: Beside is not enough. The text names the box only from inside a label, or through `for` and `id`.

choices.text: "checkbox, checked" and nothing else
choices.why: Right. With no label the box has no name, so the student hears what it is and not what it is for.

choices.text: Nothing, because the reader skips a box with no label
choices.why: The box is still announced; it is announced without a name.

choices.text: The `id` of the input, in place of a name
choices.why: An `id` on its own names nothing; it only matters when a label's `for` points at it.

prompt: The student ticks the guitar session and reloads the page. Put what happens in order.
hint: From the click, through the rules and the watcher, to the second visit.
items: `sessions.value` is replaced with the new list
The watcher writes the list to `localStorage`
The reload reads the list back from the browser

prompt: Match each field to what `v-model` reads and writes for it.
hint: The kind of field chooses what the same directive does.

prompt: Each row of a list keyed by index has an input with `v-focus`. The first item is removed from the list. Does the directive's `mounted` hook run again?
hint: Which keys survive the removal, and what does Vue do with a component whose key survives?

choices.text: Yes, on every row, because the list was replaced
choices.why: A new list does not mean new elements. Vue compares keys, and keys 0 and 1 are still there.

choices.text: Yes, on the row whose item moved up into position 0
choices.why: That row's element was already on the page as key 0. It is updated with a new item, not mounted.

choices.text: No: keys 0 and 1 survive, so their elements are updated, not mounted again
choices.why: Right. The only element that changes its life is key 2, and it is removed, which runs `unmounted` rather than `mounted`.

choices.text: No, because a directive's hooks run once per application
choices.why: They run per element: `mounted` would run for any element newly put on the page, which removing one does not do.

prompt: Which of these does the planner's list of the week use? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the template of the new list.

choices.text: `v-for` with `:key="session.id"`
choices.why: Right. A real key, the session's id.

choices.text: `v-model` on each checkbox
choices.why: The box is bound by hand, with `:checked` and `@change`, so that the change goes through `toggle`.

choices.text: `v-if` and `v-else` for a week with nothing planned
choices.why: Right. One paragraph for an empty week, the list otherwise.

choices.text: `v-show` on the paragraph for an empty week
choices.why: It is `v-if`, which pairs with `v-else`; `v-show` does not work with `v-else`.

choices.text: `:class="{ done: session.done }"` on each row
choices.why: Right. A session that is done gets the class that strikes it through.
